criteria.note: Ball valves with red handles and water meters are visible in an open floor access hatch.
Two red-topped lever handles are clearly visible on the pipes, plus small white handles on the meter-side valves.
No drips, water or stains are visible on the valves or pipes in the open hatch.

rows.note: Flat's tiled access hatch: two red-lever ball valves, filters and water meters, no visible leak or stains. Lever position must not be judged.

criteria.note: A blue ball valve is visible below the water meter, though cropped at the bottom.
A blue lever handle is visible at the bottom of the frame, partly cut off.
The visible valve body and fittings look dry, with no drips, water or stains.

rows.note: Outdoor meter with a blue-lever ball valve below; the valve is partly cut off at the bottom edge, so a retake is defensible.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter's display and housing, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible in the photo.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve with its handle, usually on the pipe near the water meter, with the whole valve in frame.
rows.note: Electronic water meter lying on a table, not installed; no shut-off valve in frame.

criteria.note: Several shut-off valves are visible on the outdoor pipe manifold beside the water meters, though some are partly behind plants.
A small valve handle is visible at the left pipe, and other handles show on the vertical pipe.
No obvious drips, but the black-and-white image and plants make stains or corrosion hard to judge.

rows.retakeHint: Retake in colour, closer to the flat's own valve, with plants moved aside and good light so stains or rust can be seen.
rows.note: Black-and-white outdoor wall with several meters and small valves of a shared building; which valve is the home's is unclear and corrosion can't be judged in B/W. Corroded pipework makes fix_first defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter dial, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible; only the meter face is in frame.
No valve is in frame, so the valve area can't be judged for leaks or stains.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve on the pipe next to the meter, with its handle or lever in view.
rows.note: Close-up of a dirty meter dial, no valve in frame (sample photo).

criteria.note: This is an outdoor excavation with a water meter box and pipe fittings, not the flat's own shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever can be seen on the buried pipe fittings.
No valve is in frame, and the pipe fittings are too small and dirty to judge for leaks.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the flat's own indoor shut-off valve, such as under the sink or in the utility cupboard, with the handle clearly in frame.
rows.note: Street excavation with the utility's meter box, lid closed, no lever visible; wrong subject (the valve is inside the building).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve is visible on a copper pipe against the wall.
A metal lever with a green grip is clearly visible beside the valve.
No drips, water stains or corrosion visible; only ordinary solder and patina on the pipe.

rows.note: Brass ball valve with a green lever on copper pipe, clean (sample photo).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve is visible between copper pipes with soldered joints.
A dark green lever handle with a metal base hangs below the valve.
No drips, water or stains seen at the valve or joints; only ordinary patina and solder.

rows.note: Brass ball valve on copper pipe with a black lever; the lever position is ambiguous but never judged.

criteria.note: Only a close-up of a braided hose section is shown; neither the valve nor the machine end is in frame.
No shut-off valve is visible in this close-up of braided hose.
The braid looks intact here, but the connections are not visible, so the whole hose can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and show the whole hose from the wall valve to the washing machine, with both connections and the valve in frame.
rows.note: Macro of a braided steel hose only: neither the machine nor its tap is in frame.

criteria.note: Only a braided hose section is in frame; the machine end is cut off and the photo is mostly out of focus.
Only part of a valve fitting is visible at the bottom, cut off and blurred; the whole shut-off valve is not shown.
The visible braided hose and lower fitting show no drips or stains, but the connections are blurred or cut off.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and take one sharp photo showing the whole hose, from the wall valve to the machine, with the valve fully in frame.
rows.note: Braided hose into a chrome angle valve, shallow focus; no machine in frame, so the hose is not visible from tap to machine.

criteria.note: A white P-shaped sink trap is clearly visible in frame.
A stream of water is dripping from the bottom of the trap.

rows.fix: Clean the drain or trap: lift off the cover, remove hair and dirt, and rinse. If a nut leaks, tighten it.
rows.note: White plastic sink trap with water dripping from it: leak at the trap, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: Photo shows a loose brass valve part held in hand against bricks, not an installed dishwasher connection.
Only a detached brass fitting is shown, not an installed dishwasher shut-off valve.
No installed hose or connection is visible, so leaks cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed dishwasher hose and shut-off valve under the sink or behind the appliance, with the fittings in frame.
rows.note: A hand holding a loose brass valve with thread tape: a loose part, not an installed connection. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Under-sink white plastic waste pipe with a bottle-style trap and connectors is visible.
No drips, standing water or stains visible on the trap, joints or cabinet floor.

rows.note: Open under-sink cupboard: plastic trap with an appliance branch, dry clean floor, no leak. (No drip tray, but that is L4, not L5.)

criteria.note: Under-sink cabinet is open, but a person's body blocks the view; only a small white pipe piece is seen at the top.
The trap area is hidden, so leaks or blockage cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take the photo with nothing blocking the view, so the whole sink trap and pipes under the sink can be seen.
rows.note: A person lying in an open sink cupboard (legs only); the trap is not clearly visible. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Only the sink strainers are visible from above; the trap is hidden behind closed cabinet doors, and no floor drain is in view.
The trap and pipework can't be seen, so leaks there can't be judged. The sink basin shows no standing water.

rows.retakeHint: Open the cabinet door under the sink and photograph the trap and pipes from the front, with good light.
rows.note: Kitchen with the lower cupboard doors closed; the trap is not visible (sample photo).

criteria.note: This shows a braided hose from a toilet cistern or basin, not a dishwasher connection.
An angle valve is visible, but it serves a toilet or basin, not a dishwasher.
No drips, water, stains or kinks visible on the hose, fittings or valve.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the hose and shut-off valve under the kitchen sink where the dishwasher connects, showing the whole connection.
rows.note: Toilet supply: braided hose and angle stop valve under a toilet cistern; wrong appliance for the dishwasher check.

criteria.note: A distribution board with rows of ABB breakers and cover panels fills the frame.
Covers are in place and no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts are visible.
Several RCDs with round TEST buttons and blue levers are visible on the left and lower right.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.note: Modern ABB board: RCDs with TEST buttons, B16 breakers, labelled circuits, cover on (sample photo).

criteria.note: An old electricity meter board with fuse holders is visible in a recess.
Fuse covers and caps are removed and lying loose, with wiring and terminals exposed.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible, only an old meter and fuse holders.
Tools, fuse covers and parts are placed in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old single-phase installation with porcelain screw-fuse holders, a removed fuse and tools on the floor: exposed parts, no RCD.

criteria.note: An empty distribution board enclosure and its cover are visible, but no devices are installed.
Empty unused enclosure with the cover removed; this does not show an installed, working board, so damage can't be judged.
No RCD or any other devices are installed on the DIN rail.
Cover is off and plastic-wrapped item rests on the cover; this is not a normal installed board.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph your installed, fully fitted fuse box with its cover on, showing the breakers and RCD with its TEST button.
rows.note: An empty consumer-unit enclosure with its cover beside it, bare DIN rail, no breakers: not an installed board. fix_first (missing cover, no RCD) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A distribution board with breakers and wiring is fully in frame.
The board has no front cover, so wiring and terminals are exposed.
Three RCBO units are visible, each with a TEST button area.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Consumer unit with its front cover removed: RCBOs and exposed terminals, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: A wall-mounted breaker panel with its door open is clearly in frame.
The cover is in place, with no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts visible.
Two breakers at positions 6 and 12 have yellow TEST buttons, which look like GFCI/AFCI type devices.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the panel.

rows.note: US breaker panel, door open, dead front on, handwritten circuit numbers, two GFCI breakers with TEST buttons (residual-current protection).

criteria.note: Only a single isolated RCD device is shown, not a fuse box or distribution board.
The device looks intact, but the board itself is not shown so this can't be judged.
An RCD with a TEST button is clearly visible.
No board in view, so the area in front of it can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the real item, not a screen or a printed photo.
rows.note: Product photo of an ABB RCD on a white background: not the home's board.

criteria.note: An old industrial distribution board with several enclosed switch and fuse boxes is fully in frame.
Heavy rust, worn paint and dents are visible on the panel and housings; covers appear in place, no exposed live parts seen.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible; only old switch and fuse enclosures.
Nothing is stored in front of the board; only its own cables hang across it.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old industrial cast-metal switchgear (ASEA) with covers on but no RCD visible. A retake (not a home board) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A grey metal distribution board with its door open is clearly in frame.
Door is open and fuse holders, terminals and bare wiring are exposed; some loose wires and a cable run near the top.
Only fuses, a meter and a small breaker are visible; no RCD with a TEST button can be seen.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Open metal cabinet in an outbuilding: meter, screw fuses, main switch and exposed empty fuse bases; RCD not clearly visible.
